trial_name: TARGET Protein — Augmented Enteral Protein During Critical Illness (2025)
citation: Summers MJ, Chapple LS, Karahalios A, Bellomo R, Chapman MJ, Ferrie S, et al; TARGET Protein Investigators; Australian and New Zealand Intensive Care Society Clinical Trials Group. Augmented enteral protein during critical illness: the TARGET Protein randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2025;334(4):319-328.
one_liner: Routine substitution to an isocaloric higher-protein enteral formula increased protein delivery but did not improve 90-day hospital-free survival or mortality in unselected adult ICU patients.

pico.population: Adult ICU patients (≥16 years) prescribed enteral nutrition during their index ICU admission or a subsequent ICU admission within the same index hospital admission.
pico.intervention: Isocaloric higher-protein enteral formula (Nutrison Protein Intense; 100 g protein/L, 1.0 kcal/mL) as the default formula during intervention periods.
pico.comparison: Usual-protein enteral formula (Nutrison Protein Plus; 63 g protein/L, 1.0 kcal/mL) as the default formula during control periods.
pico.outcome: Days free of the index hospital and alive at day 90 (primary outcome); 90-day survival, ICU/hospital length of stay, duration of ventilation, tracheostomy, new renal replacement therapy (secondary).

background.existing_knowledge: Critical illness is characterized by severe catabolism, muscle wasting, and persistent functional disability. ICU nutrition guidelines recommend relatively high protein delivery targets, but routine practice often achieves substantially less. Observational studies linking higher protein delivery to improved outcomes are confounded by survivorship bias.
background.knowledge_gap: Randomized evidence for augmented protein has been limited and heterogeneous in dose, timing, and co-interventions, leaving uncertainty about benefit, harm, and subgroups.
background.hypothesis: Routine substitution to an isocaloric, higher-protein enteral formula would increase the number of days free of the index hospital and alive at day 90.

methods.design: Investigator-initiated, pragmatic, cluster-randomised, cross-sectional, double cross-over, open-label trial in 8 mixed adult ICUs in Australia and New Zealand, with staggered commencement in 2 strata.
methods.setting: 8 adult ICUs; each ICU participated for 12 months with 3-month cluster periods. 4 ICUs commenced 23 May 2022, 4 commenced 23 Aug 2022 (delayed start stratum). Outcomes derived from ICU registry and hospital administrative data.

inclusion: Prescribed enteral nutrition during index ICU admission, or prescribed EN for the first time during a subsequent ICU admission within the same index hospital admission
exclusion: ≥12 hours of non-trial enteral nutrition already delivered in ICU

methods.intervention: Augmented protein formula (Nutrison Protein Intense; 100 g protein/L, 1.0 kcal/mL) as the default; initiated when clinicians commenced EN, with rate and caloric targets per local practice; continued until ICU discharge, death, or day 90. Patients remaining in ICU across crossover dates continued their original formula; readmissions within 90 days resumed the original formula.
methods.comparison: Usual protein formula (Nutrison Protein Plus; 63 g protein/L, 1.0 kcal/mL) under identical clinician-driven feeding rates/targets; rescue feeding strategies and co-interventions permitted and recorded.
methods.blinding: Unblinded at bedside (formula-level intervention); primary outcome and mortality derived from administrative/registry data, limiting detection bias; open-label delivery creates risk of performance bias for nutrition delivery and discharge-related outcomes.
methods.sample_size_power: 8-cluster, 4-period crossover design; cluster-period size ≥60 provides 80% power, ≥80 provides 90% power to detect a 1-day difference in days free of index hospital and alive at day 90 (assumptions: within-cluster within-period correlation 0.02; cluster autocorrelation 0.8; 2-sided α=0.05).
methods.primary_outcome: Days free of the index hospital and alive at day 90 (death or ongoing hospitalisation yields 0 days).
secondary_outcomes: Length of ICU stay (time to live ICU discharge)
Duration of invasive ventilation (among ventilated patients)
New kidney replacement therapy during index ICU admission

headline_bullets: Protein delivery was higher in the augmented group (median 1.33 vs 0.84 g/kg IBW/day excluding enrolment day) with similar caloric intake (17 vs 17 kcal/kg IBW/day).
The primary outcome—days free of index hospital and alive at day 90—was not different: median 62 vs 64 days, median difference –1.97 days (95% CI –7.24 to 3.30, P=0.46).
90-day survival was similar (72.6% vs 74.0%, RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.95–1.03).
ICU discharge was modestly slower in the augmented group (cause-specific HR 0.93, 95% CI 0.88–1.00) but hospital discharge and ventilator duration were not significantly different.

Pre-specified subgroup interactions suggested possible harm in patients with new RRT at formula commencement (interaction P<0.001) and an opposite-direction effect by invasive ventilation status (interaction P=0.02), but these are hypothesis-generating.

outcomes_table.outcome: Days free of index hospital and alive at day 90
outcomes_table.note: Primary outcome; quantile mixed model with bootstrap 95% CI.

outcomes_table.outcome: Days free of index hospital at day 90 (survivors only)
Length of ICU stay (time to live ICU discharge)
outcomes_table.note: HR <1 indicates slower discharge; competing risk analysis.

outcomes_table.outcome: Length of hospital stay (time to live hospital discharge)
Duration of invasive ventilation (hours, among ventilated patients)
outcomes_table.note: No clear effect on ventilator duration.

outcomes_table.outcome: New kidney replacement therapy during index ICU admission

subgroup_table.subgroup: New kidney replacement therapy at formula commencement
subgroup_table.note: Interaction P<0.001; moderate credibility (ICEMAN). Effect direction suggests possible harm in those already on RRT.
Median difference in ventilated patients –3.44 days, in non‑ventilated +2.70 days; interaction P=0.02. Not adjusted for multiplicity.

safety: Serum urea at day 10 was higher in the augmented protein group: median 13.0 mmol/L (IQR 8.3–21.3) vs 10.6 mmol/L (7.2–17.6).
New renal replacement therapy was similar (7.3% vs 7.4%, RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.81–1.16).
Overall, there were no other signals of major harm; adverse events beyond renal were not systematically reported.

domains.notes: Cluster-level randomisation of ICUs to intervention sequences reduced contamination risk. Allocation was revealed to sites in advance for operational reasons, creating potential anticipatory behaviour at cluster transition points. Staggered commencement and period effects were modelled in the primary analysis.

Open-label delivery could influence feeding behaviours, interruptions, and co-interventions. Primary outcome and mortality were objective and derived from administrative/registry data, limiting detection bias. Discharge‑related outcomes remain susceptible to system pressures and clinician behaviour.

3411 enrolled, 3397 analysed for primary outcome (14 withdrew consent, 12 augmented vs 2 usual). ITT analysis with high data completeness due to registry/administrative capture. Missingness mainly affected weight-based delivery metrics.

Protocol deviations: 9.4% augmented vs 5.6% usual (clinician choice of non‑trial formula). Audit episodes: correct trial formula used in 66% of audits; crossover patients continued originally assigned formula, reducing within‑patient contamination.

Well balanced: age 60.8 vs 60.5 years, APACHE II score 19 vs 19, BMI 27.7 vs 27.4. High acuity: invasive ventilation 82.4% vs 79.0%, vasopressors 55.3% vs 55.0%. Time to EN start ~19 hours in both groups.

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is moderate to strong. The cluster crossover design with objective primary outcome and minimal attrition supports robust inference. Main threats are open-label delivery (performance bias for feeding/discharge) and discharge‑outcome susceptibility to non‑physiological factors.

domains.notes: Broad adult ICU inclusion with few exclusions (formula contraindication, >12h prior non‑trial EN). High rates of mechanical ventilation and vasopressor use mirror typical ICU EN recipients. Excludes complex GI/surgical phenotypes or patients requiring specialised formulas.

Pragmatic substitution of a specific isocaloric formula pair; generalisable to units in high‑resource systems using 1 kcal/mL polymeric formulas with similar baseline protein delivery. Less generalisable where protein is routinely delivered at higher baseline levels, where protein modules/parenteral amino acids are systematically used, or where caloric targets differ materially. Does not test protein combined with mobilisation or anabolic interventions.

external_validity.verdict: Generalisability is good to adult ICUs in similar high‑resource settings with comparable enteral feeding practices. Extrapolation is limited for settings with markedly different protein delivery paradigms or for phenotypes requiring longer/higher‑intensity protein exposure.

strengths: Large, pragmatic, multicentre evaluation (n=3397) with unit‑level implementation and minimal disruption to routine care.
Cluster crossover design minimises between‑unit confounding and contamination typical of individual randomisation for formula‑level interventions.
Isocaloric formulas enabled a focused test of protein augmentation without confounding by energy delivery.
Patient‑centred primary outcome with objective ascertainment via administrative/registry linkage and 90‑day follow‑up.
A priori protocol and statistical analysis plan, with explicit modelling of clustering/period effects and pre‑specified subgroup credibility assessment.
limitations: Open-label delivery; clinician‑driven feeding rates, interruptions, and co‑interventions could dilute or distort treatment effects.
Achieved protein dose depends on weight scalar: by actual body weight, median protein delivery remained below many guideline targets (1.04 vs 0.64 g/kg ABW/day excluding enrolment day).
Median exposure to the trial formula was relatively short (87 vs 84 hours), limiting potential impact on longer‑term recovery outcomes.
Primary outcome constrained to the index hospital: readmissions/transfers outside the index hospital were not captured, potentially affecting precision of hospital‑free days.
Discharge‑related outcomes are sensitive to health‑system capacity and non‑physiological influences.

critical_appraisal.summary: A well‑conducted pragmatic cluster crossover trial that answers a focused clinical question with a patient‑centred outcome. Internal validity is moderate due to open‑label delivery and discharge‑related endpoints; external validity is good for similar ICU settings. The neutral result, combined with consistent evidence from other recent trials, challenges the notion that universal early protein escalation improves recovery.
strengths: Robust cluster crossover design with a priori analysis plan
Isocaloric formula separation of protein from energy
Objective, 90‑day, patient‑centred primary outcome with minimal attrition
Pragmatic, real‑world implementation across multiple centres
weaknesses: Relatively short median exposure to the trial formula
Discharge outcomes influenced by health‑system factors

sections.authors_conclusion: Routine substitution to an isocaloric higher‑protein enteral formula increased delivered protein substantially but did not improve 90‑day hospital‑free survival. These data do not support a one‑size‑fits‑all default to high‑protein formulas for unselected adult ICU patients solely to improve downstream hospital‑free survival.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: This trial does not support routine use of a high‑protein enteral formula for all ICU patients. The decision to augment protein should be individualised, particularly considering renal function and timing.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult ICU patients receiving enteral nutrition in comparable high‑resource settings where baseline protein delivery is similar.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Protein is harmful; it only means that uniform early escalation does not improve hospital‑free survival. Higher protein may still benefit specific subgroups not yet identified.
implementation_caveats: Achieved doses may still be below many guideline targets, especially when using actual body weight; the trial cannot rule out benefit from higher doses or longer exposure.
Patients with acute kidney injury or on RRT may be harmed by higher protein; renal phenotype should be considered.
Long‑term functional outcomes and quality of life were not measured, so the net effect on patient‑centred recovery remains uncertain.
This trial tested early formula substitution, not a comprehensive protein strategy (e.g., combination with mobilization, timing‑based dosing).

controversies.topic: Interpretation of delivered protein dose (weight scalar debate)
controversies.notes: Correspondence argued that median delivered protein (1.04 vs 0.64 g/kg ABW/day) was below guideline targets, potentially testing moderate vs low rather than high vs standard protein. The trialists countered that the comparison reflects real‑world practice; using ideal body weight, doses were 1.33 vs 0.84 g/kg IBW/day, closer to guideline recommendations, and energy intakes were well matched.

Augmented protein raised serum urea (13.0 vs 10.6 mmol/L at day 10). A pre‑specified subgroup suggested fewer hospital‑free days in patients with new RRT at enrolment (median difference –13.19 days, interaction P<0.001). Post‑hoc EFFORT Protein data echo potential harm in acute kidney injury, supporting urea‑based risk stratification.

controversies.topic: Consistency with other trials and meta‑analyses
controversies.notes: EFFORT Protein and PRECISe both found no improvement with higher protein strategies; PRECISe even reported lower health‑related quality of life. An updated systematic review and meta‑analysis with trial sequential analysis concludes ongoing uncertainty about benefit or harm, reinforcing the need for phenotype‑ and timing‑specific trials.

context_related_trials.relation: Higher vs usual protein dosing in ICU; also found no benefit on time to discharge alive or other clinical endpoints, consistent with TARGET Protein.

High‑protein strategy (≥2.0 g/kg/day) focused on functional recovery; reported no benefit in physical function and worse health‑related quality of life in the high‑protein arm, reinforcing concerns about harm from aggressive protein early in illness.

unresolved_questions: What is the optimal timing of protein delivery (early vs delayed)?
Can renal phenotype (urea trajectory, RRT status) identify patients who benefit from or are harmed by higher protein?
Is there a benefit from higher protein doses when combined with structured early mobilization or anabolic agents?
Would longer exposure (>~3.5 days) to augmented protein improve longer‑term functional recovery or quality of life?
What weight scalar (actual, ideal, or adjusted) best defines an adequate protein dose in critical illness?

numbers_to_remember: Primary outcome: median hospital‑free days 62 vs 64 (median diff –1.97, 95% CI –7.24 to 3.30, P=0.46)
ICU discharge HR: 0.93 (95% CI 0.88–1.00, slower with augmented protein)
Subgroup: new RRT interaction P<0.001 (potential harm)
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Routine substitution to a high‑protein enteral formula in unselected ICU patients does not improve 90‑day hospital‑free survival; universal early protein escalation should be avoided, especially in renal dysfunction.
